e.t: “Athens” is the name of a prominent city in Greece. In the New Testament, the word identifies Athens as a specific geographical place rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. It occurs four times, all in Acts and 1 Thessalonians. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what was happening in Athens on each occasion, but the word itself simply names the city. e.t: This word means “to pull up,” describing the action of bringing something upward or drawing it out. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 13:48. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains the upward pulling or drawing of something. The word therefore points to a definite physical action expressed in the sentence.

e.t: This word means “to appear”—to come into view or become visible. It describes something or someone presenting itself openly so that it can be seen. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Luke 19:11 and Acts 21:3. Its basic sense concerns appearance or visibility, while the surrounding verse determines what appears and how that appearance functions in the sentence. It is therefore a straightforward word about becoming visible or coming into view, rather than a term whose meaning depends on a specialized religious idea.

This Greek New Testament word means “cousin,” referring to a family relative who is not a sibling. It is a noun naming that relationship. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Colossians 4:10, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word identifies a person by family connection rather than by occupation, action, or character.

This word describes apostasy—a turning away from a former allegiance, commitment, or position. It refers to departure rather than a simple change of place, and its sense is naturally understood as abandoning what one had previously identified with or followed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 21:21 and 2 Thessalonians 2:3. The surrounding passage determines precisely what allegiance or position is being abandoned in each occurrence.

e.t: This word means “filled,” “to fill,” or “was filled,” describing something being made full or becoming full. It functions as a verb, expressing the action or result of filling a person, container, place, or other thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times across seven verses, including descriptions of boats, jars, crowds, and other things becoming full. Its exact sense—whether an instruction to fill something or a statement that something has been filled—depends on how it functions in the sentence.

e.t: This word means “to train”: to develop ability or readiness through repeated practice and discipline. It describes a process that forms a person so that a desired response becomes stronger and more reliable. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, including places where people are described as trained or needing training. The surrounding verse determines whether the training concerns conduct, discernment, endurance, or another area of life; the central idea remains purposeful formation through practice.

e.t: This word means “to gain” or “to gain in trade.” It describes obtaining an increase or profit, especially through commercial activity or the use of entrusted resources. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:15, and functions as an action word describing what someone obtained. Its central idea is not merely possessing something, but gaining an added return from what was available or entrusted. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself points clearly to successful increase or profit.

This word means “peace,” or describes something “of peace.” It names peace as a central condition or quality in New Testament speech, whether presented as something given, possessed, proclaimed, or contrasted with conflict. The word appears 92 times in the Greek New Testament, across 85 verses, showing that peace is a recurring biblical subject rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This word means “handed over,” describing someone or something being delivered into another person’s hands or control. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 2:23. The word itself expresses the act of transfer or surrender; the surrounding verse determines who hands over whom and the precise force of that act. Its central idea remains a deliberate or completed giving over to another party.

Elmadam is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 3:28, within the genealogy recorded there. Because it functions as a name, its main purpose is identification: it distinguishes this person from the other individuals named in the genealogy. The word itself does not provide a separate description of the person’s character or role.

e.t: This word means “to walk among” or “to walk in/among.” It describes movement through or presence within a group, place, or surrounding setting. The wording focuses on being among something or someone rather than standing apart. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 6:16. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is movement or activity within an environment or community.

e.t: This word means “to call on” someone or “to intercede,” describing an appeal made on behalf of another. It can refer to addressing or petitioning someone, especially when one person acts as an advocate for others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Acts, Romans, and Hebrews. Its precise emphasis—calling upon someone or interceding for someone—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “be rejected” or “to be rejected.” It describes being refused or not accepted, focusing on rejection rather than acceptance. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 9:12. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the wider context, while its basic meaning remains the experience of being rejected.

This word means “longed for,” describing someone who is eagerly wanted and deeply cherished. It expresses strong desire for a person’s presence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 4:1, so its meaning is represented by a single occurrence rather than a wide range of passages. The surrounding verse determines precisely how this longing is expressed there, but the word itself points to people who are greatly wanted and held in strong affection.

This Greek New Testament word means “necessary” or “needful,” describing something required or genuinely needed. It points to what a person lacks or what circumstances call for, rather than something merely preferred or convenient. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in James 2:16, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that verse depends on the sentence and wider passage.

Quietness means a calm, undisturbed state rather than noisy or disruptive activity. It describes being quiet in conduct or manner, and can also express the peaceful condition a person is to maintain. This Greek New Testament word occurs four times, each in a different verse, and is consistently rendered “quietness.” Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject. The word appears in Acts, 2 Thessalonians, and 1 Timothy.

James is a personal name used for several men in the Greek New Testament. It identifies people rather than describing a quality, action, or object. The name occurs 42 times in 38 New Testament verses, including passages naming followers of Jesus and other believers. Because it is a name, its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage and the person being discussed. It appears from Matthew through Jude and is consistently rendered “James.”

e.t: This word means “to dishonor”—to treat someone or something as lacking the honor, respect, or good standing that should be given. It can describe bringing disgrace upon another person or being put to shame. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 13 times, so its central idea is consistent across several settings: dishonor is the opposite of honoring, and it may be expressed by words or actions that lower someone’s dignity or reputation.

This word refers to a person’s behavior—the way that person lives and conducts himself or herself. It describes outward conduct as a recognizable pattern of life, rather than a single isolated act. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 2:3, so its exact emphasis there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central sense remains the observable manner in which someone lives. [p03:word:greek-nt:G2688:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G2688:occurrences] [p01:word:greek-nt:G2688:reference:0]

Cinnamon is the meaning of this Greek New Testament word. It names cinnamon itself, a specific substance rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament corpus, at Revelation 18:13. Since the verse text is not included here, the word’s ordinary referent can be stated clearly without assigning additional contextual significance to that passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “dust,” referring to the fine particles of earth that can cling to a person’s feet, clothing, or surroundings. It is an ordinary noun for physical dust, not a special religious term. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Luke, and Acts. Its plain meaning is therefore straightforward: loose, dry earth or dirt found on the ground and carried from place to place.

Lazarus is a personal name. In the Greek New Testament, it identifies people called Lazarus rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 15 times in 15 verses, occurring in Luke and John. It is used in Luke 16 and repeatedly in John 11–12, so its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage. As a name, its meaning is simply the identification of Lazarus in the biblical account.

e.t: This word means “to practice magic” or “to practice sorcery.” It describes engaging in magic as an activity, rather than simply referring to a magical claim or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 8:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the practice of sorcery or magic. This meaning is distinct from merely being amazed by supernatural activity or hearing someone make impressive claims.

This word means “sword,” referring to a bladed weapon used for fighting, defense, or execution. It is a noun describing a physical weapon, whether one sword or several. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 29 times, so its basic meaning remains consistent across passages. Scripture may use a sword in direct accounts of armed conflict, while some passages use the image of a sword to speak of division or judgment; the surrounding verse determines that particular force. The word itself, however, names the weapon rather than the larger lesson drawn from it.

e.t: This word means “to send for” or “to summon”—to call someone to come, usually by sending a message or request. It describes an action directed toward another person rather than simply speaking to someone who is already present. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, all in Acts, and its normal sense remains consistent: arranging for a person to come or calling that person to appear. The surrounding passage determines who is summoned and why, but the word itself emphasizes the call or request that brings someone there.

e.t: This word means “to hire”—to obtain someone’s work by agreeing to employ them. It describes the action of bringing workers into service, rather than the workers themselves or the payment they receive. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both in Matthew 20, where the same word is rendered “hire.” Its precise force in either verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of hiring or employing someone.

The word means “death.” It names death itself rather than an action or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 4:19 and 2 Corinthians 4:10. The available verse references identify where it appears, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so its precise force in either passage depends on the sentence and context. Its central lexical meaning remains death.

This word is the personal name “Noah,” referring to the biblical figure named in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears eight times in eight New Testament verses, including passages in Matthew, Luke, Hebrews, and Peter. Its exact significance in any particular sentence comes from the surrounding passage.

Passover is the name of the biblical observance remembered and discussed in the New Testament. As a noun, it identifies the feast itself rather than an action or personal quality. The word appears 29 times in the Greek New Testament, across 27 verses, showing that it is used repeatedly for this recognized occasion. Its meaning remains specific: Passover, the established feast referred to in passages from Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and Hebrews.

This word means “five thousand,” naming a quantity of five thousand people or things. It is a number word, used in the Greek New Testament to state an amount rather than describe a person, action, or spiritual quality. It occurs six times in the Greek New Testament, in passages recorded in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Its normal meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse identifies what is being counted.

“Rocky” describes ground or terrain covered with or marked by rocks. In the Greek New Testament, this adjective occurs four times, all in Matthew and Mark. Its clearest ordinary sense is physical: it identifies a place whose surface or structure contains rock, making it distinct from ordinary soil. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself expresses the condition “rocky.”

This word means a stone tablet or tablets—a flat piece of stone used as a writing surface. It refers to physical tablets rather than writing in general. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing twice in 2 Corinthians and once in Hebrews. Its ordinary meaning remains concrete: a durable stone surface on which words or commandments may be written or preserved. The precise significance of the tablets in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

The word means “Rabboni,” a title or form of address. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only twice, in Mark 10:51 and John 20:16. The English rendering also preserves it as “Rabboni,” so the term is presented as a distinctive address rather than translated into a broader English description. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This word means “silk” or “made of silk,” describing a valuable textile or something produced from that material. It identifies the material itself rather than expressing an action, emotion, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 18:12. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains the fine fabric known as silk.

This word refers to a “tabernacle” or “tent”—a dwelling place formed as a tent. It can describe an ordinary temporary shelter or the tabernacle associated with worship, depending on the surrounding passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 20 times, including references to tents, the tabernacle in Israel’s history, and God’s dwelling. Its basic idea remains a tent-like dwelling place rather than an action or quality.

This word means “grapes,” referring to the fruit that grows in clusters on a vine. It is a plural term for grapes rather than for a single grape. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times: in Matthew, Luke, and Revelation. The word itself identifies the fruit; its particular significance in any passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This word means “to stir up”—to arouse, agitate, or move something into active disturbance. It describes an action that unsettles or excites people or circumstances rather than leaving them calm and still. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 6:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense is the deliberate stirring of others or of a situation.

e.t: This word means giving testimony alongside another witness or testimony that confirms what has already been declared. The idea is not merely speaking, but bearing witness together so that the testimony is supported or jointly affirmed. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in Hebrews 2:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to testimony that accompanies and confirms another witness.

Timaeus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Mark 10:46. The word’s meaning is simply “Timaeus”; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain the person’s role in that specific scene. Thus, readers should understand it as a name identifying someone, not as a general theological or descriptive term.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “severely” or “more severely,” describing how strongly or intensely something happens. It functions as an adverb, modifying an action or condition rather than naming a person, object, or event. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:23. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is a heightened degree of severity or intensity.

This word refers to a light-bearing object—a light, lights, or a star. It describes something that shines or gives visible light, rather than light understood only as an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing this clear sense in two different passages. Its ordinary meaning is therefore a shining body or source of light, with the surrounding verse determining exactly what kind of light-bearing object is meant.

This word means “place,” referring to a particular location or area. It is a noun used for a physical spot identified in relation to people or events. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times across 9 verses, including references to places in Matthew, Mark, John, and Acts. Its basic sense remains broad: it can identify any distinct location, whether a named area or a spot described by what happens there. The surrounding verse determines which specific place is intended.

e.t: This verb means “to sow above” or “to sow afterward.” It describes the act of placing seed after or over something, depending on the sentence’s context. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 13:25. The word focuses on the action of sowing and indicates that the action follows or is performed over something already present. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.
